title: Rankine and Kelvin: Absolute Temperature Scales
h1: Rankine and kelvin — the two absolute temperature scales
description: Kelvin is SI. Rankine is US customary. Both start at absolute zero. Here is why chemical engineers in the US still use Rankine and how to convert.

hero: Kelvin sizes its degree like Celsius. Rankine sizes its degree like Fahrenheit. Both start at absolute zero. Chemical engineers switch based on what units the rest of their equations use.
body: The kelvin (K) is the SI absolute temperature. The Rankine (°R) is its Fahrenheit-sized counterpart. Both are needed because thermodynamic formulas — ideal gas law, Stefan-Boltzmann, Clausius-Clapeyron — require an absolute temperature, and mixing an absolute with a relative scale gives nonsense.

Kelvin: everywhere except US thermodynamics textbooks. Rankine: US chemical, mechanical and petroleum engineering, especially when the rest of the calculation is in Fahrenheit and psi. Steam tables in US units are Rankine. Steam tables in SI units are kelvin.
## Ideal gas law in both systems

SI: PV = nRT with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). US: PV = nRT with R = 10.73 psi·ft³/(lbmol·°R). Same physics, different unit-consistent gas constants. Mixing them — using °F instead of °R — introduces a 459-unit offset error that swamps any signal.
## Worked example — ideal gas density at 70°F, 14.7 psi
Kelvin: SI absolute, Celsius-sized degree. Rankine: US absolute, Fahrenheit-sized degree. °R = °F + 459.67. Always use absolute temperature in thermodynamic formulas.

faqs.a: 0 K = −273.15°C = −459.67°F = 0 °R. Point at which all classical thermal motion ceases. Unattainable, but modern laser cooling reaches within nanokelvin.

faqs.q: Do engineers actually still use Rankine?
faqs.a: Yes, especially in US HVAC, refrigeration, oil & gas process engineering. Any steam or gas calculation in US units uses Rankine.
The unit name 'kelvin' is lowercase (like 'metre'). The symbol 'K' is capitalised (honouring Lord Kelvin). No degree sign — never '°K'.
